sources.headline: Rubio says US not 'under systemic attack' after series of tech outages
sources.text: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot."We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple. Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor. Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people."Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said.Cybersecurity experts say there is no evidence connecting the Microsoft, airline, and bank disruptions from the last five days.Kris Beevers, CEO and co-founder of the network and infrastructure management company NetBox Labs, acknowledged the circulating theories on social media linking the barrage of outages."There is no conspiracy here," he told the BBC."There is something more ordinary, and more important to understand: the infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change is risk. Much of it is 30 to 40 years old, with decades of technical debt, and it's now being asked to change very quickly."Beevers said AI is only part of the story."It's putting more strain on these legacy networks, and it's also creating real urgency around security," he said."Our customers are the amazing teams behind these networks at airlines, banking, energy, and retail who are essentially doing heart surgery on a global scale to get these networks back up and running quickly."Vice President of Threat Intelligence for Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, Sherrod DeGrippo, said: "What this week really underscores is how tightly coupled, and fragile, our core digital infrastructure is, where a single software bug or router failure can cascade nationwide."

sources.headline: Surge in software patches likely behind recent tech outages, experts say
sources.text: WASHINGTON - While the causes of recent disruptions to the way people work, access bank accounts and travel remain unclear, increased efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered vulnerabilities in the AI age are likely a major factor, according to cybersecurity experts and US officials.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters in Manila this week, said company patching efforts are, at times, “creating short-term disruption in the way the system works.”Patches are software and operating system updates intended to fix security vulnerabilities found within a programme or product.A string of technology outages affecting airlines, workplaces and online banking has intensified concerns that organisations are struggling to keep pace with the flood of software vulnerabilities being uncovered and patched in the AI era.Banking executives said that they were rushing to fix the patches after a technical outage disrupted online operations earlier this week.Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told a House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee hearing on worldwide threats on Nov 18 that there is so far no indication that the tech outages are related.But Clayton said the speed and level of capability of computer systems are “increasing substantially,” so legacy computer systems and equipment that already were old are ageing much more quickly.The advent of easily accessible AI tools and large language models has supercharged the discovery of vulnerabilities in software.Microsoft in November has addressed more than 1,200 software vulnerabilities, nearly 20 times higher than in the same month a year ago, according to cybersecurity firm Qualys.“AI has made finding critical vulnerabilities fast and cheap, and the number of flaws that demand immediate patching has grown with it,” said Yuval Itzchakov, chief technology officer and co-founder of autonomous offensive security company A Security.“Emergency patches go into core infrastructure within hours, often without the full testing cycle, and they are intrusive by design: they change runtimes, kernels and network components that everything else depends on. That speed and scale of change is itself a source of failure,” Itzchakov said.Josh Bressers, director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure at cybersecurity firm VulnCheck, said that in 2026 there have been 100,000 publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, tracked by industry as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVEs.Of those, Bressers said, 1,363 were known to have been exploited in the real world.“Given tight resources for defenders, understanding which vulnerabilities need attention first is critical,” Bressers wrote in a LinkedIn post. “Not all vulnerabilities are created equal.”Anne Neuberger, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that AI is helping attackers find and weaponise vulnerabilities, but is a more “valuable friend” to those tasked with defending key computer networks.“AI is enabling enterprises to find 10 times more vulnerabilities,” said Neuberger, who served as deputy national security adviser under former president Joe Biden and led incident response to serious national incidents. “And when patching at scale, some can cause problems.”Bank vulnerabilitiesAt least one major bank was rushing to address a wave of recent patches and there is a lot of work needed, a source at the bank said, speaking on condition of anonymity.Lenders had also received inquiries from the banking regulator, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, after the outages, another source said.The US regulator was trying to assess the impact and also asked about increased customer communication, the source added.The OCC did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment.“The banks and everyone else have had a short-term goal on efficiency and cutting costs when it comes to AI, and that has built a technical deficit,” said John Cosgrove, head of Walden Advisory, an enterprise security and resilience advisory firm.“That might have not been a problem on its own, but AI is now introducing a speed and scale of changes that you can’t keep up with,” Cosgrove said.Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial, said technology has made banking “incredibly convenient, and while occasional outages can be frustrating, I don’t believe the outages will have a significant impact on consumer confidence or change how most people manage their money.”“Financial institutions have invested heavily in technology and security, and, unfortunately, occasional disruptions will happen,” Gestiehr said.“What matters most is how quickly those issues are identified, resolved and communicated to customers.” REUTERS
